text: Section 43A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 imposes an obligation on body corporates to implement reasonable security practices to protect sensitive personal data.
notes: Correct - Section 43A is the body corporate data protection provision

text: Section 66 of the IT Act deals with computer-related offences and provides for punishment of up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine of up to one lakh rupees.
notes: Correct - Section 66 punishes dishonest/fraudulent acts under Section 43

text: Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

text: Section 69 of the IT Act empowers the Central Government to issue directions for interception, monitoring, or decryption of any information through any computer resource.
notes: Correct

text: Section 67 of the IT Act punishes publication or transmission of obscene material in electronic form.
notes: Correct

text: Section 72 of the IT Act provides for breach of confidentiality and privacy where any person who, in pursuance of any of the powers conferred under the Act, secures access to any electronic record or information, discloses the same without consent, is punishable.
notes: Correct

text: Section 79 of the IT Act provides a safe harbour for intermediaries from liability for third-party content provided they comply with due diligence requirements.

text: The right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Constitution of India, as held by the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India.

notes: Correct

notes: Correct

notes: Correct

text: Section 43A of the IT Act requires data controllers to obtain explicit written consent from users before collecting sensitive personal data or information.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 43A itself does not require explicit written consent — this is the SPDI Rules' requirement under Rule 5, not Section 43A. The claim overstates the section's direct text.

text: Section 43 of the IT Act provides for criminal punishment of up to 5 years for unauthorized access to a computer system.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 43 is a civil remedy (compensation), not criminal punishment. Section 66 provides criminal punishment.

text: In Miranda v. Arizona (1984), the Supreme Court ruled that suspects must be read their rights.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Year is wrong. Miranda was decided in 1966, not 1984.

text: Section 66A of the IT Act is still in force and penalises offensive online speech.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 66A was struck down as unconstitutional in 2015.

text: Section 72 of the IT Act imposes criminal liability only on government officials who breach confidentiality, not private employees.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 72 applies to any person who secures access under the Act's powers — not limited to government officials.

text: 42 U.S.C. Section 1983 requires a plaintiff to prove that the defendant acted with actual malice.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 1983 does not require actual malice — it requires showing deprivation of constitutional rights under color of state law.

text: The Fourth Amendment requires police to obtain a warrant before conducting any search or seizure.
notes: HALLUCINATION: The Fourth Amendment prohibits unreasonable searches — there are numerous exceptions (exigent circumstances, plain view, search incident to arrest, etc.)

text: Section 79 of the IT Act provides absolute immunity to intermediaries for all third-party content.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 79 provides conditional safe harbour, not absolute immunity — intermediaries must comply with due diligence requirements.

text: Gideon v. Wainwright held that the right to counsel applies only to felony cases in federal court.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Gideon applied the right to counsel to state courts (not just federal), through the Fourteenth Amendment.

text: Section 66C of the IT Act punishes the hacking of computer systems and carries a penalty of up to 10 years imprisonment.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 66C covers identity theft (not hacking), with punishment of up to 3 years, not 10.

text: The Supreme Court's exclusionary rule was established in Weeks v. United States for state courts.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Weeks applied the exclusionary rule to federal courts; it was extended to state courts by Mapp v. Ohio (1961).

text: Section 67 of the IT Act requires the government to prove actual harm to public morality to obtain a conviction.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 67 punishes publication of obscene material without requiring proof of actual harm — the test is whether the material is obscene under the Hicklin/contemporary community standard.

text: The right to privacy declared in Puttaswamy is an absolute fundamental right that cannot be restricted by any law.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Puttaswamy held privacy is a fundamental right BUT subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2) and proportionality test — not absolute.

text: Section 43A applies to government bodies that handle sensitive personal data of citizens.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 43A applies to body corporates (private entities) — government departments are excluded from the SPDI Rules.

text: The Miranda warning must be given in all police encounters, including routine traffic stops.
source: Miranda v. Arizona / Berkemer v. McCarty
notes: HALLUCINATION: Miranda applies only to custodial interrogation. Routine traffic stops are not custodial.

text: Section 66A was struck down because it violated the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 66A was struck down for violating Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech), not Article 14.

text: In Terry v. Ohio, the court required probable cause for an investigatory stop.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Terry established the reasonable articulable suspicion standard, which is lower than probable cause.

text: Section 69 of the IT Act requires a court order before the government can intercept any electronic communication.
notes: HALLUCINATION: Section 69 allows executive direction by the Central/State Government without a court order.

text: Section 70A of the IT Act established the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) as the national nodal agency for cybersecurity.
notes: HALLUCINATION: CERT-In is established under Section 70B, not 70A.

text: The Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution was enacted in 1870 to grant voting rights to freed slaves.
notes: HALLUCINATION: The Fourteenth (1868) granted citizenship and equal protection. The Fifteenth (1870) granted voting rights.
